> **What this case shows** — the sway–cognition cases used the **Falls Efficacy Scale (FES)** total, a
> summed fear-of-falling score. A summed score is only meaningful if the items hang together. The
> **newly-authored** `cronbachAlpha` measures that internal consistency across 163 BDS subjects,
> reproducing base R, **`psych::alpha`** **bit-for-bit** and **`pingouin.cronbach_alpha`** to machine
> precision. The 7 FES items have **good internal consistency (α = 0.82**, mean inter-item r = 0.41) — they
> measure one coherent construct.

::: {.callout-tip title="The recipe you'll learn"}
**Workflow** — a respondents × items matrix → `cronbachAlpha()` → read α and the mean inter-item correlation.
**Way of thinking** — before you sum a questionnaire into one score, check that its items are consistent.
Cronbach's alpha asks "do these items co-vary as if they measure the same thing?" — a prerequisite for
treating the total as a single number, and a different question from the signal analyses elsewhere.
**Ecosystem usage** — `PhysioAnalysis::cronbachAlpha()`.
:::

## Proposition

The 7 Falls Efficacy Scale items in the BDS cohort (n=163) have Cronbach's raw α = 0.823 (mean inter-item
correlation 0.41), i.e. good internal consistency; `cronbachAlpha` reproduces `psych::alpha` (raw_alpha)
bit-for-bit and `pingouin.cronbach_alpha` to machine precision.

## Question & goal

**The question is a prerequisite made explicit: is the FES total a legitimate single score?** The
sway–cognition cases leaned on the summed FES; this fold certifies that the items are internally consistent
enough to sum, and authors a psychometric reliability op.

## Challenge & approach

We take the 163 × 7 matrix of FES item responses (4-point Likert), compute `cronbachAlpha` from the item and
total-score variances, and check α and the mean inter-item correlation against `psych::alpha` and
`pingouin.cronbach_alpha`.

```
163 subjects × 7 FES items → cronbachAlpha
  raw alpha = 0.823   (mean inter-item r = 0.41)   ->  "good" (> 0.8)
     vs psych::alpha raw_alpha        → |diff| = 0 (bit-for-bit)
     vs pingouin.cronbach_alpha       → |diff| ~ 1e-16 (machine precision)
```

## Data

**Santos & Duarte (2016) BDS balance dataset (figshare)**: the seven Falls Efficacy Scale items (FES_1..FES_7,
concern about falling during daily activities), for the 163 subjects. Details in
[`artifacts/data_sources.json`](artifacts/data_sources.json).

## Results

![Left: the 7×7 inter-item correlation matrix of the FES items — uniformly positive correlations (mean r=0.41) as expected for a consistent scale. Right: Cronbach's α = 0.82 against the conventional benchmarks — above the "good" (0.8) line, below "excellent" (0.9).](artifacts/figure.png)

*How to read this:* left — every pair of items is positively correlated, none near zero, so no item is
pulling against the rest. Right — α clears the "good" threshold, supporting use of the summed total.

| Quantity | Value |
|---|--:|
| **Cronbach's α** | **0.823** (good) |
| mean inter-item correlation | 0.41 |
| items / respondents | 7 / 163 |
| vs `psych::alpha` (\|diff\|) | **0** (bit-for-bit) |
| vs `pingouin.cronbach_alpha` (\|diff\|) | **< 1e-9** (~1e-16) |

α equals psych exactly and pingouin to machine precision. Values trace to
[`artifacts/cronbach_summary.csv`](artifacts/cronbach_summary.csv).

## Conclusion

`cronbachAlpha` reproduces the reference and broadens the ecosystem into psychometrics. The transferable
takeaway: **when you reduce a questionnaire to a total, certify its internal consistency first. Here α=0.82
justifies treating the seven FES items as one fear-of-falling score — the same score the sway–cognition
cases correlate with balance. Reliability is a prerequisite, checked, not assumed.**

## Open questions

- Alpha establishes internal consistency, not dimensionality or validity; a factor analysis would confirm
  the FES is unidimensional, and item-total / drop-one-alpha statistics would flag any weak item. Alpha also
  rises with item count. The single raw-alpha here is the standard first-line reliability check. *Documented,
  not escalated.*

## Using this in your own analysis

| Step | Function | Package |
|---|---|---|
| Internal-consistency reliability | `cronbachAlpha()` | PhysioAnalysis |
| Correlation among items | `correlationTest()` | PhysioAnalysis |

**Reading the result.**

- **α** — internal consistency (0–1); conventional bands are ~0.7 acceptable, 0.8 good, 0.9 excellent.
  Report it before summing items into a score.
- **mean inter-item r** — a scale-length-independent companion to α; ~0.15–0.5 is typical for a coherent
  but not redundant scale.

**The recipe, copy-runnable:**

```r
library(PhysioAnalysis)

cronbachAlpha(fes_items)   # respondents x items matrix -> alpha + mean inter-item r, bit-for-bit vs psych::alpha
```

**Auditing the numbers.** Every value on this page traces to
[`artifacts/cronbach_summary.csv`](artifacts/cronbach_summary.csv), and [`audit.py`](audit.py) re-checks the
alpha and the mean inter-item correlation, the bit-exact match against psych and the machine-precision match
against pingouin, the good-reliability threshold, the item/respondent counts, and the honestly noted scope
(authors the new cronbachAlpha op; a self-report scale, not a signal; reliability is consistency, not
validity).
